learn: The ladder of tagging methods and the most-frequent-tag baseline
Word embeddings, character embeddings and out-of-vocabulary words
Recurrent taggers: RNNs, LSTM gates and Bi-LSTMs
The Bi-LSTM-CRF and a fully worked CRF sequence score
Why per-token accuracy overstates sentence quality
Fine-tuning BERT/RoBERTa with a linear head, and subword alignment
Prompting LLMs to tag (zero- and few-shot)
LLM agents that use a tagger as a tool, and comparing all methods
intro.why: This session follows tagging from hand-built probability models to the methods used in practice today. The same ladder (embeddings → recurrent encoders → CRF → Transformers → prompting → agents) describes how nearly every NLP task has modernised.

sections.title: A ladder of methods and the unigram baseline
sections.plain: Each new method uses more of the sentence, more directly; the starting point uses none of it.
sections.body:
The question that runs through the whole session: how much of the sentence can the model use, and how cheaply?

methodcontext usedtraining≈ accuracy (Penn-style)
Most-frequent-tag (unigram) baselinenonelookup≈ 90–92%
HMM / MEMM / CRFa few nearby tagslight≈ 95–96%+
Bi-LSTM-CRFwhole sentence, both directionsmedium, sequential≈ 97–98%
Fine-tuned Transformerwhole sentence, in parallelpre-train + fine-tune≈ 98.5–99.5%
LLM promptingeverything it has readnonehigh but variable
LLM agent with a tagger toolplan + the toolnonethe tool's accuracy

Worked baseline: "She books a flight ." Suppose "books" is NNS 70% of the time in training. The baseline tags She/PRP books/NNS a/DT flight/NN ./. and gets 4 of 5 tokens right, missing the one that matters (VBZ). A pronoun before and "a + noun" after make the verb reading obvious to any model that reads neighbours.

sections.title: Word and character embeddings
sections.plain: Represent each word as a vector; build extra vectors from spelling so unseen words still get a sensible input.
sections.body:
Word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe; M3) give each known word a fixed vector, so what the tagger learns about one word transfers to similar words. Similarity is measured with cosine: with king = [0.9, 0.8], queen = [0.85, 0.9], cat = [−0.7, 0.6]: cos(king, queen) = 1.485/(1.204 × 1.238) ≈ 0.996; cos(king, cat) = −0.15/(1.204 × 0.922) ≈ −0.135.

Character embeddings: a small network (character CNN or LSTM) reads the word letter by letter. Suffixes (-ly → adverb, -ing → verb form, -tion → noun), prefixes and capitalisation become evidence, which rescues out-of-vocabulary words. The token input is the concatenation [word part ; character part], e.g. [0.9, 0.8, −0.2, 0.1 ; 0.7, −0.3].

Static embeddings give "bank" one vector in every context; that's acceptable here because the encoder above adds context. Contextual embeddings (BERT) remove the issue.

sections.title: RNN and LSTM taggers
sections.plain: Read the words in order with a learned memory; run one pass each way and join their summaries.
sections.body:
A simple RNN keeps a running summary $h_t = g(W x_t + U h_{t-1} + b)$ and predicts a tag from each $h_t$. Over long sentences early information fades (vanishing gradients). The LSTM adds a cell state with three sigmoid gates:

$$f_t = \sigma(W_f x_t + U_f h_{t-1} + b_f),\ i_t = \sigma(\dots),\ g_t = \tanh(\dots),\ o_t = \sigma(\dots)$$$$c_t = f_t\odot c_{t-1} + i_t\odot g_t,\qquad h_t = o_t\odot\tanh(c_t)$$

Worked scalar step ($c_{t-1}$ = 0.5, $h_{t-1}$ = 0.3, $x_t$ = 1.0): f = σ(0.72) = 0.673; i = σ(0.69) = 0.666; g = tanh(0.76) = 0.641; c = 0.673·0.5 + 0.666·0.641 = 0.763; o = σ(0.65) = 0.657; h = 0.657 · tanh(0.763) = 0.422. (Picture minutes of a meeting: keep decisions that still matter, jot new points, read out what's relevant.)

A Bi-LSTM runs a forward and a backward LSTM and concatenates $[\overrightarrow h_t; \overleftarrow h_t]$, so each word's vector reflects both its left and right context ("river bank ." vs "bank account").

sections.title: BiLSTM-CRF and a worked CRF score
sections.plain: Let the encoder score each tag per word, add learned tag-to-tag scores, and pick the best whole sequence.
sections.body:
Per-word softmax ignores that tags constrain each other (DT is rarely followed by a verb). A linear-chain CRF layer scores whole sequences:

$$\text{Score}(t_{1:n}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} E_i[t_i] + \sum_{i=2}^{n} T[t_{i-1}\to t_i],\qquad P(t_{1:n}) = \frac{\exp\text{Score}}{Z},\ Z = \sum_{\text{all } t'}\exp\text{Score}(t')$$

Emissions E come from the Bi-LSTM; transitions T are learned. Training raises the true sequence's score relative to Z (computed with the forward algorithm); decoding uses Viterbi.

Worked: "the plays". E(the) = DT 5, NN 0, VBZ −2; E(plays) = DT −3, NN 2, VBZ 3. T[DT→NN] = 4, T[DT→VBZ] = −1 (full table in the lab). Greedy per word: DT VBZ, score 5 − 1 + 3 = 7. Best path: DT NN, 5 + 4 + 2 = 11. Over all nine paths Z ≈ 61,402.9, so P(DT NN) = e¹¹/Z ≈ 0.975 and P(DT VBZ) ≈ 0.018. The transition reward outweighs VBZ's larger emission.

sections.title: Token vs sentence accuracy
sections.plain: A small per-word error rate becomes a large chance that a long sentence contains a mistake.
sections.body:
Bi-LSTM-CRF reaches about 97–98% per token on Penn Treebank-style data with no hand-written features, and transfers well to low-resource languages; its drawback is slow, sequential training.

If each token is correct with probability a independently, an n-word sentence is entirely correct with probability aⁿ:

  • a = 0.97, n = 20: 0.97²⁰ = e^{20 ln 0.97} = e^{−0.609} ≈ 0.544.
  • a = 0.99, n = 20: 0.99²⁰ ≈ 0.818.

On a million tokens: 30,000 errors at 97% vs 10,000 at 99%, a threefold cut. Errors aren't truly independent, so aⁿ is an estimate, but it explains why the last percent matters and why sequence-level metrics (exact match) are reported alongside token accuracy.

sections.title: Self-attention for tagging
sections.plain: Each word directly gathers information from every other word, weighted by relevance.
sections.body:
The Transformer replaces sequential reading with self-attention. Each token gets a query q, key k and value v (learned projections):

$$\alpha_j = \text{softmax}_j\Big(\frac{\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf k_j}{\sqrt d}\Big),\qquad \text{output} = \sum_j \alpha_j\mathbf v_j$$

Worked: tagging "bank" (d = 2): q = [1, 2]; keys river [1, 2], the [2, 0], "." [0, 1]. Scores 5, 2, 2 → ÷√2 → 3.54, 1.41, 1.41 → softmax 0.807, 0.097, 0.097. Values river [0, 1], the [1, 0], "." [0.5, 0.5] → output [0.145, 0.855]: a strong noun signal, drawn mostly from "river". The cost is the same whether "river" is 1 or 50 words away.

Multi-head attention runs several such heads in parallel; stacking heads with feed-forward layers forms an encoder (M11). Attention costs O(n²) in sentence length, and attention weights show what was looked at, not the final decision.

sections.title: Fine-tuning BERT and subword tokens
sections.plain: Start from a Transformer pre-trained on huge text and add a one-layer tag classifier on each token.
sections.body:
BERT and RoBERTa are pre-trained with masked language modelling (predict hidden words from both sides), so they already encode syntax. For tagging, add a linear head on each token's contextual vector h and fine-tune everything for a few epochs:

$$\text{logits} = \mathbf W\mathbf h + \mathbf b,\qquad P(t) = \frac{e^{\text{logit}_t}}{\sum_{t'}e^{\text{logit}_{t'}}}$$

Worked: "plays" in "she plays well": h = [0.5, −1.0, 2.0, 0.3]; rows DT [0.1, 0.2, −0.5, 0], NN [0.3, 0.1, 0.4, −0.2], VBZ [−0.2, −0.3, 0.9, 0.5] → logits −1.15, 0.79, 2.15 → softmax 0.029, 0.198, 0.773: VBZ.

Subwords: rare words split into pieces ("playing" → play + ##ing). Convention: predict the tag on the first piece and ignore the others in the loss; otherwise words and labels drift out of alignment. Fine-tuned Transformers reach ≈ 98.5–99.5% and are the default in spaCy and Hugging Face pipelines. They are also parallel: a 50-word sentence needs 50 sequential RNN steps but roughly one parallel step per Transformer layer.

sections.title: Prompting LLMs to tag
sections.plain: Describe the task in words; add a few solved examples to lock the output format and tagset.
sections.body:
A large language model can tag with no task-specific training. Zero-shot: "Tag the following sentence using the Penn Treebank tagset. Output only the word/tag pairs. Sentence: The concert was great." Expected: The/DT concert/NN was/VBD great/JJ ./. A typical slip is the right grammar with the wrong vocabulary (great/ADJ or great/adjective).

Few-shot: prepend examples in the exact format ("Dogs/NNS bark/VBP ./." and "She/PRP left/VBD ./.") and the model copies the convention, returning great/JJ.

Cautions: off-tagset or hallucinated tags, inconsistent tokenisation of punctuation, cost and latency per call, and output that must be parsed and validated. For high-volume, accuracy-critical tagging a fine-tuned Transformer remains cheaper and steadier; prompting shines for quick prototypes, rare languages or tagsets, and mixed tasks.

sections.title: Agentic pipelines and comparing methods
sections.plain: An LLM plans a bigger job and calls a specialised tagger as a tool for the precise step.
sections.body:
An LLM agent is a language model that can call tools (function calling). The loop: read the request → break it into steps → call a tool where needed → read the tool's output → finish the task.

Worked: "Analyse the sentiment of all nouns in the user reviews." Plan: find nouns (needs exact tags), find what describes each, report. Tool call POS_tag("The battery is amazing but the screen is dull .") → battery/NN, screen/NN, with adjectives amazing/JJ and dull/JJ. Result: battery +0.8, screen −0.6. The LLM supplies planning and the write-up; the tagger (e.g. fine-tuned BERT) supplies precision.

Choosing a method: fine-tuned Transformer for accuracy and volume; Bi-LSTM-CRF or CRF where compute is tight; prompting for zero-data prototypes; agents when tagging is one step of a larger task. Risks in agents: mis-planning, misreading tool output, and cost per call. POS tagging on clean benchmark text is close to solved; the open problems are noisy domains (social media, code-mixed text), low-resource languages, and using tags well downstream.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Benchmarks vs reality: 99% on newswire can drop sharply on tweets or transcribed speech; evaluate in-domain.
  • Do LLMs need POS tags? Rarely as explicit input, but tags remain useful for search, extraction, linguistics and explainable pipelines.
  • CRF on top of BERT often adds little for POS (the encoder already captures dependencies) but can help NER, where label constraints (I-PER after B-PER) are strict.
  • Distillation: a small tagger trained on an LLM's or large model's outputs can be cheap at inference.

code.title: Embeddings, an LSTM step and a CRF
code.explain: Computes cos(king, queen) = 0.996 and cos(king, cat) = −0.135, the scalar LSTM step (f 0.673, i 0.666, g 0.641, o 0.657 → c 0.763, h 0.422), and all nine CRF path scores for 'the plays' with Z ≈ 61,402.9, P(DT NN) = 0.975 and the Viterbi best path.
code.notes: Scores are log-potentials; probabilities come only after dividing by Z.
code.code:
"""Embeddings, one LSTM step, and a CRF over 'the plays' (brute force, Z, and Viterbi)."""
import numpy as np
from itertools import product

# 1. Cosine similarity of tiny embeddings
E = {"king": np.array([0.9, 0.8]), "queen": np.array([0.85, 0.9]), "cat": np.array([-0.7, 0.6])}
cos = lambda a, b: a @ b / np.linalg.norm(a) / np.linalg.norm(b)
print(f"cos(king, queen) = {cos(E['king'], E['queen']):.3f}; cos(king, cat) = {cos(E['king'], E['cat']):.3f}")

# 2. One scalar LSTM step
sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
c_prev, h_prev, x = 0.5, 0.3, 1.0
f = sig(0.5 * x + 0.4 * h_prev + 0.1)
i = sig(0.6 * x + 0.3 * h_prev)
g = np.tanh(0.7 * x + 0.2 * h_prev)
o = sig(0.4 * x + 0.5 * h_prev + 0.1)
c = f * c_prev + i * g
h = o * np.tanh(c)
print(f"LSTM: f={f:.3f} i={i:.3f} g={g:.3f} o={o:.3f} -> c={c:.3f}, h={h:.3f}")

# 3. Linear-chain CRF on 'the plays'
tags = ["DT", "NN", "VBZ"]
Em = {"the": [5, 0, -2], "plays": [-3, 2, 3]}
T = np.array([[-2, 4, -1], [-1, 1, 3], [2, 2, -3]])  # row = from, col = to
words = ["the", "plays"]
scores = {}
for a, b in product(range(3), repeat=2):
    scores[(tags[a], tags[b])] = Em["the"][a] + T[a, b] + Em["plays"][b]
for k, v in sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]):
    print(f"  {k[0]:3s} {k[1]:3s}: {v:+d}")
Z = sum(np.exp(v) for v in scores.values())
print(f"greedy per word: {tags[int(np.argmax(Em['the']))]} {tags[int(np.argmax(Em['plays']))]} (score {scores[('DT','VBZ')]})")
print(f"Z = {Z:.1f}; P(DT NN) = {np.exp(11)/Z:.3f}; P(DT VBZ) = {np.exp(7)/Z:.3f}")

# Viterbi in score space (sums, max)
v = np.array(Em["the"], dtype=float); 
v2 = np.array([max(v[a] + T[a, b] for a in range(3)) + Em["plays"][b] for b in range(3)])
best_b = int(np.argmax(v2)); best_a = int(np.argmax([v[a] + T[a, best_b] for a in range(3)]))
print(f"Viterbi: {tags[best_a]} {tags[best_b]} with score {v2[best_b]:.0f}")

code.title: Attention, a BERT-style head, sentence accuracy and an agent pipeline
code.explain: Reproduces the 'bank' attention weights (0.807/0.097/0.097, output [0.145, 0.855]), the tagging head (VBZ 0.773), 0.97²⁰ vs 0.99²⁰, and a toy plan → tool → integrate pipeline in which a lexicon stands in for a fine-tuned tagger.
code.notes: The 'tool' is a stand-in; a real system would call a trained tagger.
code.code:
"""Self-attention for 'bank', a BERT-style tagging head, sentence accuracy, and a tiny tool-using pipeline."""
import numpy as np, re

# 1. Scaled dot-product attention for the query 'bank'
q = np.array([1, 2]); K = {"river": [1, 2], "the": [2, 0], ".": [0, 1]}; Vv = {"river": [0, 1], "the": [1, 0], ".": [0.5, 0.5]}
s = np.array([q @ np.array(k) for k in K.values()]) / np.sqrt(2)
a = np.exp(s) / np.exp(s).sum()
out = sum(w * np.array(Vv[k]) for w, k in zip(a, K))
print("scaled scores:", np.round(s, 2).tolist(), " weights:", np.round(a, 3).tolist(), " output:", np.round(out, 3).tolist())

# 2. Classification head on a contextual vector for 'plays'
h = np.array([0.5, -1.0, 2.0, 0.3])
W = {"DT": [0.1, 0.2, -0.5, 0.0], "NN": [0.3, 0.1, 0.4, -0.2], "VBZ": [-0.2, -0.3, 0.9, 0.5]}
logits = {t: float(np.array(w) @ h) for t, w in W.items()}
Zs = sum(np.exp(v) for v in logits.values())
print("logits:", {t: round(v, 2) for t, v in logits.items()}, " probs:", {t: round(float(np.exp(v) / Zs), 3) for t, v in logits.items()})

# 3. Token vs sentence accuracy and error counts
for acc in (0.97, 0.99):
    print(f"per-token {acc:.2f}: 20-word sentence fully correct {acc**20:.3f}; errors per 1M tokens {round((1-acc)*1e6):,}")

# 4. An 'agent' pipeline: plan -> call a tagger tool -> use the tags
LEX = {"the": "DT", "battery": "NN", "screen": "NN", "is": "VBZ", "but": "CC", "amazing": "JJ", "dull": "JJ", ".": "."}
def pos_tag(sentence):                      # the 'tool' (stand-in for a fine-tuned tagger)
    return [(w, LEX.get(w.lower(), "NN")) for w in re.findall(r"\w+|[^\w\s]", sentence)]
POLARITY = {"amazing": 0.8, "dull": -0.6}   # stand-in sentiment lexicon
review = "The battery is amazing but the screen is dull ."
plan = ["find nouns with the POS tool", "find the adjective describing each noun", "report sentiment per noun"]
print("plan:", " -> ".join(plan))
tags = pos_tag(review); print("tool output:", " ".join(f"{w}/{t}" for w, t in tags))
for k, (w, t) in enumerate(tags):
    if t == "NN":
        adj = next((x for x, tt in tags[k + 1:] if tt == "JJ"), None)
        print(f"  {w}: described as '{adj}', sentiment {POLARITY.get(adj, 0):+.1f}")
